record.paper_title: Current Unsolved Problems in Planetary Nebulae Research
record.original_question: Why does the bright-end cutoff of the planetary-nebula luminosity function appear nearly invariant across extragalactic stellar populations of very different ages when stellar-evolution models still struggle to reproduce that invariance completely, especially in old populations where star formation ceased more than about 5 Gyr ago?

evidence.quote: Models of stellar evolution have had difficulty explaining this invariance: they predict more planetary nebulae at luminosities above the cut-off, and a lower cut-off in older systems.
The faster evolution shown by the new post-AGB stellar evolution models [170] has resolved part of the discrepancies [186] but not all [187].

artifact.self_contained_problem:
The planetary-nebula luminosity function (PNLF) is the distribution N(M) of planetary nebulae as a function of absolute magnitude M in the [O III] λ5007 emission line. Empirically, the PNLF in a wide variety of galaxies is well described, near its bright end, by a function that truncates sharply at an absolute magnitude M*, and the value of M* is observed to be remarkably similar (within a few tenths of a magnitude) across host stellar populations whose mean ages differ by an order of magnitude — from young, star-forming spiral disks to old elliptical galaxies in which star formation effectively ceased more than ~5 Gyr ago.

Standard stellar-evolution theory predicts that planetary nebulae descend from asymptotic-giant-branch progenitors whose central-star mass, post-AGB luminosity, and post-AGB transition timescale all decrease with the age of the parent population. As a consequence, the predicted [O III] luminosity of the brightest planetary nebulae in a coeval population should decrease substantially with population age, producing a fainter PNLF cutoff M* in old systems and (under some assumptions) an excess of nebulae brighter than the observed cutoff in young systems. Even when one incorporates the faster post-AGB evolution given by modern post-AGB tracks (which shortens transition times for low-mass cores and partially raises their peak luminosities), a fully self-consistent stellar-evolutionary mechanism that reproduces the observed near-invariance of M* across all population ages — and in particular accounts for the existence of [O III]-bright planetary nebulae in stellar populations older than ~5 Gyr — has not been established.

Problem. Provide a quantitative physical/stellar-evolutionary model of single-star and/or binary post-AGB evolution, together with the associated nebular ionization and (if relevant) circumstellar/circumnebular dust extinction, that predicts the bright-end cutoff M* of the [O III] λ5007 PNLF as a function of progenitor mass and population age, and show that this model reproduces the observed near-constancy of M* across stellar populations ranging from young (≲1 Gyr) to old (≳5–10 Gyr), including the existence of planetary nebulae with [O III] luminosities at or near M* in old, quiescent populations.
artifact.status_search_result: The age-invariance of the PNLF bright-end cutoff has been a long-standing puzzle. Faster post-AGB evolutionary tracks (Miller Bertolami 2016) showed that lower-mass, longer-lived central stars can reach higher luminosities, partially closing the gap, and recent work (2025) argues that circumnebular dust extinction in younger populations, together with revised post-AGB tracks, plays a critical role in maintaining a near-invariant cutoff. However, a fully consistent explanation accounting for [O III]-bright planetary nebulae in old (>5 Gyr) populations is not yet established, and recent VLT-MUSE PNLF studies (2025) of early-type galaxies continue to investigate residual stellar-population dependence. The problem is therefore best characterized as partially solved.

status_evidence.title: The mysterious age invariance of the planetary nebula luminosity function bright cut-off
status_evidence.snippet: The cut-off value appears to be nearly the same for different stellar populations... a vexing issue that has persisted for the past 35 years.
status_evidence.claim: The age invariance of the PNLF bright cutoff is a long-standing unresolved problem.

status_evidence.title: The Critical Role of Dust on the [O III] PNLF Bright-end Cutoff (2025)
status_evidence.snippet: Dust is perhaps the driving force behind the invariance of the PNLF's bright-end cutoff; higher-mass cores experience greater circumnebular extinction.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work proposes circumnebular dust extinction as the key mechanism producing the invariance, partially resolving the issue.

status_evidence.title: Towards precision cosmology with improved PNLF distances using VLT-MUSE — III (2025)
status_evidence.snippet: Impact of stellar populations in early-type galaxies on the PNLF.
status_evidence.claim: Stellar-population dependence of the PNLF in old galaxies is still under active investigation in 2025.
